### The new regime: the Product Liability Directive

Directive (EU) 2024/2853, adopted 23 October 2024, entered into force on 8 December 2024, but applies only to products placed on the EU market from 9 December 2026 onward. Unlike the withdrawn proposal, it establishes strict liability: an injured party need not prove fault, only that the product was defective, that damage occurred, and that a causal link exists between the two.

Key features specific to AI:

Software as a product. For the first time in the history of EU product liability law, software – including AI systems – is explicitly treated as a product rather than a service. AI providers accordingly take on manufacturer status and fall under the same liability regime as manufacturers of physical goods.

Presumption of defect. If a manufacturer refuses a court-ordered request to disclose technical documentation about an AI system, the court may presume the product was defective. This materially eases an injured party’s position in disputes involving opaque or complex AI systems, whose operation a claimant often cannot independently reconstruct or prove.

No contractual exclusion. Article 15 of the Directive expressly prohibits excluding or limiting liability for damage caused by a defective product by contract. This matters in particular for businesses operating on a software-as-a-service model, which routinely include liability-limitation clauses in their terms – such clauses will have no legal effect against liability under this directive.

Manufacturer status on substantial modification. Article 25 of the AI Act provides that a party who substantially modifies a high-risk AI system belonging to someone else assumes manufacturer status – and, consequently, liability under the Product Liability Directive – for that modification. This is particularly relevant for companies that customize or integrate third-party AI systems into their own products or services.

What stays outside the directive’s scope. Pure economic loss – the most common outcome in B2B disputes involving AI – is not compensable damage under this directive, nor are privacy infringements or discrimination. These continue to be governed by the national tort law of individual member states, which varies significantly from one jurisdiction to another.

### 3. The mediating doctrine constraint

 The third surviving channel is not a compensation route in its own right, but a body of regulatory duties that shape civil proof and the standard of care through national mediating doctrines. That constraint should be stated with precision. The AI Act and the MDR do not themselves determine civil liability. They do not convert non-compliance into automatic defect or automatic negligence. Nor does compliance create civil immunity. Their role is mediated. They affect what evidence exists, what warnings and instructions were supplied, what oversight architecture was expected and what a court may regard as relevant to safety expectations or reasonable clinical care.Footnote 
<sup>32</sup>

 A concrete illustration may be taken from AI Act Article 14 on human oversight. Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks that persist despite other requirements.Footnote 
<sup>33</sup>
 In a negligence claim involving S2 or S3, that provision does not compel an Irish, Italian or German court to treat any departure from Article 14 as negligence per se. But it can inform the court’s assessment of what the institution and the producer side knew or should have known about foreseeable automation bias, alert reliance, or the need for meaningful human verification. The same is true, in a partially different register, for MDR requirements on information supplied with the device and post-market surveillance. Those requirements do not answer the negligence question. They shape the evidential and normative environment within which the negligence question is asked.Footnote 
<sup>34</sup>

 This mediating role is especially important because human oversight has become one of the main conceptual bridges between ex ante risk regulation and ex post civil liability. Scholarship has already noted that “human oversight” is both legally attractive and operationally unstable. It can be used to justify continued human responsibility even where system design channels user behaviour in strong ways. In the healthcare setting, that instability is visible where a radiology triage tool re-orders worklists, a deterioration system normalises response to alert architecture, or an ambient scribe generates a persuasive note that a time-pressured clinician then signs. The oversight requirement is therefore relevant, but not dispositive. It informs the inquiry into reasonable care and foreseeable reliance. It does not settle it.Footnote 
<sup>35</sup>

### 2. The matrix, the dual-lens convention and the regulatory background

 The underlying research applies a pre-specified eight-step matrix to each scenario-jurisdiction cell. In sequence, it asks: how the system is legally classified; who controls the relevant risk points; which claimant routes are realistically available; what must be proved and by reference to which evidence; what the disclosure posture looks like; which defences are likely to matter; how remedies and procedure affect litigability; and what overall claimant position results. Practical litigability is then assessed across five dimensions: evidence accessibility, defendant complexity, expert burden, causation uncertainty and procedural friction. The purpose of this framework is not to create false quantitative precision. It is to impose a common analytical discipline across scenarios and jurisdictions, so that convergences and divergences are not disguised by shifts in narrative emphasis. A concise statement of the framework appears in the Appendix.Footnote 
<sup>12</sup>

 A second organising device is the dual-lens temporal convention. Lens A refers to Directive 85/374/EEC as transposed in national law and applies to products placed on the market before 9 December 2026. Lens B refers to Directive (EU) 2024/2853 and applies to products placed on the market or put into service thereafter.Footnote 
<sup>13</sup>
 The lens question is resolved at the classification stage before any strict-liability analysis proceeds. That sequence matters. It prevents the revised Directive from silently altering the analysis of pre-transition deployments and makes visible the extent to which the ambient-scribe scenario depends on the new Directive’s express inclusion of software supplied through network or cloud delivery as a product.Footnote 
<sup>14</sup>

 The regulatory background is likewise staged. The AI Act entered into force in 2024, but its obligations apply over time. High-risk obligations for Annex III systems apply from 2 August 2026, while the obligations relevant to Annex I regulated products, including many AI-enabled medical devices, apply from 2 August 2027. Systems already placed on the market before the relevant application date are not drawn into the later regime unless they undergo significant change thereafter.Footnote 
<sup>15</sup>
 This temporal structure is not peripheral. It means that a material installed base of healthcare AI will continue to generate evidence under earlier documentation and logging practices, and in some cases will never acquire the fuller evidential architecture associated with later AI Act compliance.
## IV. Recurrent gaps across healthcare AI claims

The structural significance of the withdrawal lies in the loss of the only EU instrument designed to address, in procedural form, the two proof problems that recur most often in AI-related harm claims: access to technical evidence held by the producer side, and causal proof under conditions of opacity and complexity.Footnote 
<sup>4</sup>
 The proposed Directive was modest. It did not offer a complete substantive theory of AI responsibility, nor did it attempt to replace national tort or medical liability law. But it did seek to alter the claimant’s position where the decisive information sat beyond ordinary access and where fault, output and harm were separated by technical mediation. The importance of its disappearance is therefore not that Europe was left with no law. It is that the claimant must now proceed through instruments that were designed for different evidential conditions.

 The article treats that post-withdrawal position as a structural fact. Existing scholarship has already shown that the revised Product Liability Directive addresses part of the software and evidential problem, and that the AI Act has shifted EU governance decisively towards *ex ante* compliance and risk management.Footnote 
<sup>5</sup>
 At the same time, recent work on civil liability and AI has continued to emphasise how distributed value chains, human oversight design and opacity complicate both fault attribution and compensation pathways.Footnote 
<sup>6</sup>
 What remains underdeveloped is a claimant-facing account of how those general observations play out in healthcare, a field in which AI systems are embedded in decision sequences that are record-dependent, multi-actor and highly sensitive to the difference between what happened, what was logged, and what can later be proved.

The thesis of this article is that, once those determinants are examined across Ireland, Italy and Germany, five structural gaps recur despite the revised Product Liability Directive and the AI Act. The reported gaps are not a free-standing taxonomy imported into the analysis. They were selected after applying the same matrix to the three archetypes in the three jurisdictions. Selection and ranking used five criteria: recurrence across the scenario-jurisdiction cells; capacity to block or materially weaken a claim rather than merely complicate it; persistence across different procedural environments; sensitivity to the revised Product Liability Directive, the AI Act and the MDR; and tractability through measures available without primary legislation. On those criteria, evidence asymmetry ranks first because every archetype depends on producer-side or cloud-held artefacts; documentation integrity ranks second because, although concentrated in the ambient-scribe scenario, absence of provenance can make attribution practically unavailable; multi-actor control ranks third because producer, deployer and clinician frequently control different risk points; warning and reliance, and causation under uncertainty follow because existing doctrines partly absorb them while leaving significant residual difficulty. The five gaps are therefore, in order of practical importance: evidence asymmetry (G1), documentation integrity (G5), multi-actor control (G3), warning and reliance (G6) and causation under uncertainty (G2). They are not evidence of legal emptiness. They are evidence of a mismatch between the evidential and organisational characteristics of healthcare AI deployments, on the one hand, and the architecture of the currently available compensation routes, on the other.Footnote 
<sup>8</sup>

The article is deliberately bounded. It is concerned with civil compensation routes and their interaction with sectoral regulation. It does not address criminal liability, professional discipline, GDPR claims as an autonomous pathway, insurance design or the full public-law enforcement architecture of the AI Act. The law-as-of date is 1 March 2026. The argument is not that the current framework is unworkable, nor that the withdrawn Directive would have solved everything. It is that the sharpest weaknesses lie at the junction between risk regulation and civil proof, and that this junction is especially visible in healthcare AI.

### 5. Implications for regulators, guidance bodies and public purchasers

 These three measures show that the most immediate response to the post-withdrawal liability landscape lies in upstream governance rather than in doctrinal development alone. That has implications for several actors. National competent authorities responsible for MDR and AI Act enforcement can treat traceability, retention and oversight design not merely as compliance matters, but as features that affect the reconstructability of harm events. Notified bodies can give closer attention to whether lifecycle documentation, instructions for use and post-market arrangements are sufficient to support patient-level incident reconstruction rather than only abstract conformity review. Guidance bodies such as HIQA-type quality agencies, the G-BA and AIFA-linked governance environments, and relevant professional bodies can frame procurement and deployment expectations in terms that connect safety governance with later accountability.Footnote 
<sup>56</sup>

 The accountability mechanisms created by the AI Act should be understood in the same setting. They include technical documentation, instructions for use, automatic logging, deployer monitoring and log retention, post-market monitoring, serious-incident reporting and, in limited Annex III settings, a right to an explanation of the AI system’s role in an individual decision. In the health sector, these mechanisms can make the relation between provider design choices, deployer use and clinical interpretation more traceable. Blatti and Tramacere’s analysis of transparency and liability in AI-based medical systems is useful here because it shows how transparency and human oversight can operate as accountability mechanisms before litigation begins, while remaining bounded by the scope of the AI Act and by the fact that regulatory accountability is not the same thing as civil liability.Footnote 
<sup>57</sup>
 For the purposes of the present article, this means that AI Act accountability mechanisms are not ignored. They are treated as part of the evidential and governance environment that can reduce opacity, support incident reconstruction and inform the standard of care through national mediating doctrines.

Large public purchasers have a particularly strong role. In concentrated markets, individual hospitals may lack leverage to insist on richer logging, provenance retention or audit access. Framework-level procurement, central guidance and collective contracting can change that bargaining position. The same is true of professional bodies that issue guidance on AI-enabled clinical tools. If their guidance remains at the level of general caution, it risks reproducing the warning-and-reliance gap. If, instead, it asks institutions to document control allocation, artefact retention and oversight realism, it can improve both governance and later legal clarity.

## V. What follows for risk regulation

### 1. An uneven but workable architecture

 The post-withdrawal landscape is uneven rather than empty. The revised Product Liability Directive improves the producer-side environment for software claims, particularly where classification, disclosure and presumptions matter. The AI Act, together with the MDR where applicable, improves the governance and evidential environment by requiring technical documentation, logs, instructions, post-market monitoring and oversight structures. Those are significant gains. Yet they do not create a general EU bridge between regulatory non-compliance and civil compensation, or displace the central role of national medical liability law, which remains the route through which most claimants will first proceed.Footnote 
<sup>52</sup>

 The unevenness is intensified by time. Many healthcare deployments already in use will not acquire richer AI Act artefacts merely because the Regulation exists. Some systems will fall outside the later high-risk obligations. Others will remain in service without the kind of significant change that would trigger application to pre-existing deployments. Still others will be formally in scope but unevenly compliant. The result is a patchwork in which some claimants benefit from richer logs, documentation and instructions, while others continue to depend on sparse records, proprietary environments and difficult counterfactuals. In that setting, risk regulation cannot be assessed only by asking whether it promotes *ex ante* safety or formal compliance. It must also be assessed by asking whether it leaves behind a litigation environment in which serious harms can be reconstructed and responsibility allocated with a reasonable degree of coherence.

### 3. G3: multi-actor control

The third gap is multi-actor control. Healthcare AI deployments distribute control across a chain of actors in ways that neither the product-liability route nor the provider-liability route maps neatly. The producer side may control design, training, performance claims and updates. The deployer may control procurement, threshold setting, workflow placement, local validation and incident response. The clinician may control final action or signature. In some cases, especially S3, a downstream clinician may act on information already shaped by the system without ever using the system directly. The legal question is not merely who caused the harm. It is which actor controlled the risk point that made the harm possible.

The structural character of G3 can be seen by comparing the scenarios. In S1, control is distributed, but the central contest is often still bilateral: producer design and updates against deployer workflow integration. In S2, threshold configuration introduces a more explicit allocation problem because the same model may behave differently depending on a parameter set locally rather than by the vendor. In S3, the chain expands again: producer-side note generation; provider-side procurement and governance; clinician review and signature; downstream clinician reliance. The ambient-scribe scenario therefore shows why control allocation is not only a product-liability issue or only a medical-liability issue. It is a chain problem.

 Ireland, Italy and Germany each provide partial but incomplete answers. Ireland’s law of concurrent wrongdoers and contribution can manage multi-defendant litigation after several parties have been joined, but it does not give a freestanding normative account of AI-mediated control allocation. Italy’s dual-track architecture is good at distinguishing institution and practitioner, but less obviously suited to integrating the producer side into the same conceptual frame. Germany’s doctrine is stronger in relation to organisational fault and to provider-side responsibility for documentation and process, but it too leaves unresolved the interface between producer control, deployer configuration and clinician use. The revised Product Liability Directive does not solve this problem, because it is still principally concerned with the producer side, even though it contains provisions on presentation as producer, related services and substantial modification.Footnote 
<sup>43</sup>
 The AI Act clarifies value-chain roles for regulatory purposes, including circumstances in which a deployer becomes a provider. But that is a public-law allocation of compliance responsibility, not a civil-law theory of multi-actor attribution.Footnote 
<sup>44</sup>

### 1. The claimant-facing problem after the withdrawal

 The withdrawal of the proposed AI Liability Directive did not create a legal vacuum.Footnote 
<sup>1</sup>
 It left in place a structured but uneven legal landscape in which a claimant who alleges harm caused by healthcare AI must route the case through three channels: strict product liability against the producer side; national fault-based liability against the provider side; and regulatory duties that matter to the evidential and normative environment, but do not themselves amount to a Union cause of action.Footnote 
<sup>2</sup>
 That architecture is workable in the limited sense that claims remain legally imaginable. It is less satisfactory in the practical sense that the route most visible to the claimant is often not the route that contains the decisive evidence. Patients usually know the hospital, clinic or the treating clinician. They rarely know who controlled the model version, the local alert threshold, the provenance trail, the audit log or the update history that later becomes determinative.

 Healthcare AI is a revealing test case because harm in this setting is usually mediated rather than immediate. In a radiology triage setting, the question is not simply whether an output was wrong, but whether the output altered worklist position, reporting time and therapeutic timing in a way that made a legally relevant difference. In a deterioration-score setting, the question is whether the model score, the local threshold and the escalation protocol altered admission, discharge or monitoring decisions. In an ambient scribe setting, the question is whether the system contaminated the medical record and whether that contamination later shaped clinical judgment. Liability therefore turns not only on AI error in the abstract, but on where the system sits in the clinical workflow, who controlled the relevant intervention point, and whether the system generated a retrievable evidential trace.Footnote 
<sup>3</sup>

### 4. G6: warning and reliance

 The fourth gap is the mismatch between formal warnings and real reliance patterns. In all three scenarios, the producer side can say that clinicians remain responsible, that outputs require review, and that the system is only assistive. In all three scenarios, the deployment may nonetheless be arranged so that the system predictably shapes clinician behaviour in ways stronger than those warnings imply. Hard worklist prioritisation makes non-prioritised cases less salient. Active alert architectures normalise reliance on the presence or absence of alerts. Auto-populated notes and medication fields reduce the intensity of human verification, especially where clinical work is fast-moving and documentation tasks are burdensome.Footnote 
<sup>45</sup>

 The structural issue is therefore not simply whether warnings existed, but whether they were consistent with the system’s real position in the workflow. This is why the gap is properly described as one of warning and reliance rather than as a simple failure of disclosure. If the system is built and deployed in a manner that makes superficial review or selective adherence foreseeable, the existence of a warning does not settle the safety or negligence question.Footnote 
<sup>46</sup>
 The revised Product Liability Directive reinforces this by expressly providing that warnings do not, by themselves, cure defectiveness. The AI Act reinforces it in a different way by requiring human oversight measures commensurate with risk, autonomy and context of use.Footnote 
<sup>47</sup>
 But neither instrument abolishes the behavioural gap. They help identify it; they do not make it disappear.

### 6. What the withdrawn Directive would and would not have solved

 The withdrawn Directive should therefore be understood with restraint. It would have addressed G1 and part of G2 by giving claimants a clearer route to producer-held evidence and by easing some causal proof under opacity. Those are precisely the points at which its absence is most clearly felt in healthcare AI cases. It would not have provided a complete theory of responsibility across the AI supply chain, and it would not have displaced the central role of national medical liability law. Multi-actor control would still have required national doctrines on negligence, contribution, organisational responsibility and clinical accountability. The Directive’s value lay in targeted procedural assistance, not in replacing that wider legal landscape.Footnote 
<sup>58</sup>

 That bounded claim matters for risk regulation. It prevents the current debate from collapsing into a false choice between “more AI-specific liability law” and “no legal problem.” The post-withdrawal framework already contains meaningful resources, and the revised Product Liability Directive and the AI Act improve the position, though unevenly. But their combination still leaves the claimant exposed where the decisive artefact sits outside ordinary reach, where provenance was not preserved, where control is distributed across several actors, and where the main negligence route still bears the weight of causal uncertainty. The task for risk regulation is therefore not only to reduce harm *ex ante*. It is also to leave behind a legal and evidential environment in which harms that do occur can be reconstructed with tolerable clarity.

On 11 February 2025, the European Commission formally withdrew its proposal for an AI Liability Directive (COM/2022/496), first presented in September 2022 as the civil-liability counterpart to the EU AI Act. The proposal was never adopted, so none of its provisions ever took effect. The withdrawal, however, does not leave a liability vacuum: liability for harm caused by artificial intelligence systems is now governed, at EU level, by the revised Product Liability Directive – Directive (EU) 2024/2853, adopted on 23 October 2024. This piece examines why the AI Liability Directive was withdrawn, what the new liability regime actually provides, and what it means in practice for businesses placing AI products or services on the EU market.

### Why the AI Liability Directive was withdrawn?

The European Commission justified the withdrawal by the absence of any realistic prospect of agreement on a final text within a reasonable timeframe – the decision was taken as part of the Commission’s 2025 Work Programme. The proposal had been built around a fault-based liability model, requiring an injured party to prove a breach on the part of the AI provider or manufacturer. The Commission concluded that the revised Product Liability Directive, which explicitly brings software – including AI systems – within the definition of a product, adequately covers the same ground, rendering a separate directive unnecessary.

The older CJEU case law retains interpretive force across the legacy regime. Veedfald confirms that a medical product can be put into circulation even in a hospital-linked context. Ford Italia reinforces the breadth of the concept of producer by presentation. Boston Scientific remains central to heightened safety expectations for medical products. Commission v United Kingdom and Commission v France continue to frame the development-risk defence by reference to the objective state of scientific and technical knowledge. Sanofi Pasteur accepts proof through serious, specific and consistent indicia rather than scientific certainty, while rejecting automatic or irrebuttable presumptions. Novo Nordisk confirms that national information-access tools may coexist with the product liability regime. Dutrueux makes clear that the harmonised product route coexists with national fault-based liability where the latter rests on a different basis.Footnote 
<sup>26</sup>
 Product liability therefore remains a viable but incomplete route for healthcare AI claims. It is strongest where the producer side is identifiable, the system is comfortably classifiable as a product, and the decisive artefacts exist and can be reached.

Lens B improves the claimant’s position in product claims through Article 10 presumptions, including the rule for excessive difficulties in establishing defectiveness or causation in technically complex cases.Footnote 
<sup>51</sup>
 That is a substantial change, especially for producer-side claims involving opaque software. But it does not extend to the negligence or treatment-contract route against the hospital, which often remains the first and most practical claimant route. The AI Act also helps only in part. Better logging can illuminate the first node in the chain, such as whether an alert fired or whether a record was generated. It does not by itself answer the later counterfactuals, whether a clinician would have acted differently, whether a different action would have occurred in time, and whether outcome would thereby have changed. G2 therefore persists because the main fault-based route continues to depend on proof structures that the new product-liability tools cannot fully reach.

The sensitivity of G5 to regulation is more differentiated than that of G1. The AI Act can reduce documentation-integrity problems substantially, but only where the system falls within scope, the relevant provisions have begun to apply, and the deployment is compliant. Article 12 requires logging, and Article 26 requires deployers to keep automatically generated logs for a minimum period.Footnote 
<sup>41</sup>
 For medical device AI, the MDR also brings traceability and post-market documentation into the picture. Recent MDCG guidance reinforces the importance of traceability, transparency and human oversight in medical device AI and links them to accountability across the lifecycle.Footnote 
<sup>42</sup>
 Yet it would be too broad to say that documentation-integrity problems disappear under the later regime. The ambient-scribe setting may fall outside MDR classification; the relevant AI Act provisions may not yet apply; and compliant high-level logging does not necessarily guarantee retention of the exact pre-edit draft or the patient-level provenance detail that litigation later demands. G5 is therefore best described as materially reducible, not removable, by later regulation.

### 2. National fault-based routes in Ireland, Italy and Germany

 The second surviving channel is national fault-based liability. In practice, it is often the first channel activated because the institution is visible, record-holding and usually solvent or indemnified. In Ireland, the relevant standard in clinical negligence remains the Dunne standard, as restated in later case law including Morrissey. Discovery under Order 31 remains comparatively broad, including the possibility of third-party discovery, although the practical and strategic value of that route in technically complex cases should not be overstated.Footnote 
<sup>27</sup>
 Irish causation remains demanding. *Philp v Ryan* and *Quinn v Mid-Western Health Board* are both relevant, but it is safer to describe them as evidence of an unsettled landscape regarding expanded causation tools than as settling any specific material-contribution doctrine for AI-mediated clinical harm.Footnote 
<sup>28</sup>

 Italy’s position is shaped by Law 24/2017. The healthcare facility is liable on a contractual footing, while the practitioner is generally liable extra-contractually under Article 2043 of the Civil Code. Product liability claims continue to proceed under the Consumer Code. The Corte di Cassazione has recently reaffirmed, in Cass. civ., Sez. III, 28 March 2025, n 8224, that the product-liability regime does not exclude or limit other liability routes, but that distinct regimes cannot simply be blended into one another. In the same decision, the Court again described product liability as a form of *responsabilità presunta*, literally “presumed liability,” rather than true objective liability.Footnote 
<sup>29</sup>
 Causation remains governed by the more-probable-than-not standard, and the court-appointed expert mechanism (*consulenza tecnica d’ufficio*, CTU) continues to play a large role in structuring medical and technical proof.Footnote 
<sup>30</sup>

## VI. Conclusion

Healthcare AI claims do not succeed or fail because of abstract positions about artificial intelligence. They turn on more concrete questions: whether the system is clearly classifiable as a product; whether the decisive artefact exists; who controlled the risk point that mattered; whether workflow design undermined formal warnings; and whether the claimant can prove a multi-step counterfactual against parties holding different fragments of the evidence. Across Ireland, Italy and Germany, those questions produce different doctrinal routes but recognisably similar structural frictions.

The revised Product Liability Directive improves the producer-side landscape for software products and for technically difficult proof. The AI Act, together with the MDR where applicable, improves the governance and evidential setting, sometimes substantially. Yet the claimant-facing weakness exposed by the withdrawal of the AI Liability Directive remains visible where evidence is vendor-held, where provenance was never retained, where control was distributed across several actors, and where negligence-side causation still carries much of the burden. The present architecture is therefore workable, but imperfect. Its sharpest weaknesses lie at the junction between risk regulation and civil proof.

 The contribution of this article is to show, through healthcare AI, that this junction is where the law now does much of its most difficult work. The post-withdrawal position is neither a void nor a complete settlement. It is an uneven architecture in which *ex ante* regulation and *ex post* compensation no longer move in step. If there is a practical lesson to draw, it is that liability readiness now depends as much on procurement design, retention architecture and workflow realism as on doctrinal elegance.

## Use of AI tools

Generative AI assistance (OpenAI ChatGPT, GPT-5.5 Pro, accessed in May 2026) was used for language revision, including grammar assistance.

### 1. Product liability under Lens A and Lens B

 The first surviving channel is strict product liability against the producer side. Under Lens A, the claimant proceeds under Directive 85/374/EEC as transposed into national law. Under Lens B, the claimant proceeds under Directive (EU) 2024/2853. In healthcare AI, the difference between the two is not merely technical. It affects whether software supplied through cloud or software-as-a-service models is comfortably classified as a product; how much procedural assistance is available where proof depends on producer-held evidence; and how the law responds to post-deployment software change, updates and continued producer control.Footnote 
<sup>18</sup>

 Under Lens B, software is expressly included as a product, whether supplied on a tangible medium or through network access, cloud or software-as-a-service models.Footnote 
<sup>19</sup>
 This matters most for the ambient clinical scribe. If the scribe is not a medical device, its treatment under Lens A remains more contestable because older national implementations were drafted against a world of tangible goods and do not uniformly resolve the status of cloud-delivered software. Under Lens B that uncertainty is greatly reduced. The revised Directive also addresses related services and substantial modification, which is relevant where functionality is altered through software updates or ongoing learning processes beyond the user’s control.Footnote 
<sup>20</sup>

 Across both lenses, the organising concept remains defectiveness, assessed by reference to the safety that a person is entitled to expect. CJEU case law has long recognised that, for medical products, safety expectations are especially demanding because the potential damage is abnormal and serious.Footnote 
<sup>21</sup>
 The revised Directive deepens the contextual analysis by making explicit that defectiveness may depend on continuing learning, interconnection with other products, cybersecurity and the circumstances of the intended user group.Footnote 
<sup>22</sup>
 It also makes clear that warnings do not, by themselves, cure defectiveness, a proposition with direct relevance to systems that are formally described as assistive but are designed in ways that predictably induce reliance.Footnote 
<sup>23</sup>

### 5. G2: causation under uncertainty

The fifth gap is causation under uncertainty. Healthcare AI harms rarely present a short path from technical event to injury. In S1, a low-priority triage output may delay review; the delay may postpone diagnosis; the postponement may or may not have altered treatment or outcome. In S2, an alert that did not fire, or did not cross a threshold, may affect escalation, monitoring or discharge; each step is contestable in clinical and evidential terms. In S3, a contaminated note may shape later clinical understanding, but only through a chain involving authorship, review, reliance and the timing of later investigation. Each of these cases requires the claimant to stabilise a counterfactual across several actors and several decision points.

 The three jurisdictions differ sharply here. Ireland remains the least claimant-friendly of the three because the but-for test continues to dominate clinical negligence, and the law is still unsettled as to how far expanded causation tools can travel in medical settings. Philp and Quinn do not resolve the matter in a way that maps neatly onto AI-mediated chains, and Morrissey does not remove that underlying difficulty.Footnote 
<sup>50</sup>
 Italy’s more-probable-than-not standard and the burden structure of Law 24/2017 soften the edges of uncertainty, especially as against the healthcare facility, but they do not by themselves solve multi-link chains involving producer-side evidence gaps. Germany offers the strongest statutory assistance through section 630h, yet even there the assistance is usually strongest on the provider side and weaker when the contested issue concerns producer-side design, provenance or calibration.

### 3. The mediating doctrine constraint

 The third surviving channel is not a compensation route in its own right, but a body of regulatory duties that shape civil proof and the standard of care through national mediating doctrines. That constraint should be stated with precision. The AI Act and the MDR do not themselves determine civil liability. They do not convert non-compliance into automatic defect or automatic negligence. Nor does compliance create civil immunity. Their role is mediated. They affect what evidence exists, what warnings and instructions were supplied, what oversight architecture was expected and what a court may regard as relevant to safety expectations or reasonable clinical care.Footnote 
<sup>32</sup>

 A concrete illustration may be taken from AI Act Article 14 on human oversight. Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks that persist despite other requirements.Footnote 
<sup>33</sup>
 In a negligence claim involving S2 or S3, that provision does not compel an Irish, Italian or German court to treat any departure from Article 14 as negligence per se. But it can inform the court’s assessment of what the institution and the producer side knew or should have known about foreseeable automation bias, alert reliance, or the need for meaningful human verification. The same is true, in a partially different register, for MDR requirements on information supplied with the device and post-market surveillance. Those requirements do not answer the negligence question. They shape the evidential and normative environment within which the negligence question is asked.Footnote 
<sup>34</sup>

 This mediating role is especially important because human oversight has become one of the main conceptual bridges between ex ante risk regulation and ex post civil liability. Scholarship has already noted that “human oversight” is both legally attractive and operationally unstable. It can be used to justify continued human responsibility even where system design channels user behaviour in strong ways. In the healthcare setting, that instability is visible where a radiology triage tool re-orders worklists, a deterioration system normalises response to alert architecture, or an ambient scribe generates a persuasive note that a time-pressured clinician then signs. The oversight requirement is therefore relevant, but not dispositive. It informs the inquiry into reasonable care and foreseeable reliance. It does not settle it.Footnote 
<sup>35</sup>

### 2. The matrix, the dual-lens convention and the regulatory background

 The underlying research applies a pre-specified eight-step matrix to each scenario-jurisdiction cell. In sequence, it asks: how the system is legally classified; who controls the relevant risk points; which claimant routes are realistically available; what must be proved and by reference to which evidence; what the disclosure posture looks like; which defences are likely to matter; how remedies and procedure affect litigability; and what overall claimant position results. Practical litigability is then assessed across five dimensions: evidence accessibility, defendant complexity, expert burden, causation uncertainty and procedural friction. The purpose of this framework is not to create false quantitative precision. It is to impose a common analytical discipline across scenarios and jurisdictions, so that convergences and divergences are not disguised by shifts in narrative emphasis. A concise statement of the framework appears in the Appendix.Footnote 
<sup>12</sup>

 A second organising device is the dual-lens temporal convention. Lens A refers to Directive 85/374/EEC as transposed in national law and applies to products placed on the market before 9 December 2026. Lens B refers to Directive (EU) 2024/2853 and applies to products placed on the market or put into service thereafter.Footnote 
<sup>13</sup>
 The lens question is resolved at the classification stage before any strict-liability analysis proceeds. That sequence matters. It prevents the revised Directive from silently altering the analysis of pre-transition deployments and makes visible the extent to which the ambient-scribe scenario depends on the new Directive’s express inclusion of software supplied through network or cloud delivery as a product.Footnote 
<sup>14</sup>

 The regulatory background is likewise staged. The AI Act entered into force in 2024, but its obligations apply over time. High-risk obligations for Annex III systems apply from 2 August 2026, while the obligations relevant to Annex I regulated products, including many AI-enabled medical devices, apply from 2 August 2027. Systems already placed on the market before the relevant application date are not drawn into the later regime unless they undergo significant change thereafter.Footnote 
<sup>15</sup>
 This temporal structure is not peripheral. It means that a material installed base of healthcare AI will continue to generate evidence under earlier documentation and logging practices, and in some cases will never acquire the fuller evidential architecture associated with later AI Act compliance.

## IV. Recurrent gaps across healthcare AI claims

---

[referencia=97a33fd2efbde2df score=0.624]
 The structural significance of the withdrawal lies in the loss of the only EU instrument designed to address, in procedural form, the two proof problems that recur most often in AI-related harm claims: access to technical evidence held by the producer side, and causal proof under conditions of opacity and complexity.Footnote 
<sup>4</sup>
 The proposed Directive was modest. It did not offer a complete substantive theory of AI responsibility, nor did it attempt to replace national tort or medical liability law. But it did seek to alter the claimant’s position where the decisive information sat beyond ordinary access and where fault, output and harm were separated by technical mediation. The importance of its disappearance is therefore not that Europe was left with no law. It is that the claimant must now proceed through instruments that were designed for different evidential conditions.

 The article treats that post-withdrawal position as a structural fact. Existing scholarship has already shown that the revised Product Liability Directive addresses part of the software and evidential problem, and that the AI Act has shifted EU governance decisively towards *ex ante* compliance and risk management.Footnote 
<sup>5</sup>
 At the same time, recent work on civil liability and AI has continued to emphasise how distributed value chains, human oversight design and opacity complicate both fault attribution and compensation pathways.Footnote 
<sup>6</sup>
 What remains underdeveloped is a claimant-facing account of how those general observations play out in healthcare, a field in which AI systems are embedded in decision sequences that are record-dependent, multi-actor and highly sensitive to the difference between what happened, what was logged, and what can later be proved.

---

[referencia=97a33fd2efbde2df score=0.596]
 The thesis of this article is that, once those determinants are examined across Ireland, Italy and Germany, five structural gaps recur despite the revised Product Liability Directive and the AI Act. The reported gaps are not a free-standing taxonomy imported into the analysis. They were selected after applying the same matrix to the three archetypes in the three jurisdictions. Selection and ranking used five criteria: recurrence across the scenario-jurisdiction cells; capacity to block or materially weaken a claim rather than merely complicate it; persistence across different procedural environments; sensitivity to the revised Product Liability Directive, the AI Act and the MDR; and tractability through measures available without primary legislation. On those criteria, evidence asymmetry ranks first because every archetype depends on producer-side or cloud-held artefacts; documentation integrity ranks second because, although concentrated in the ambient-scribe scenario, absence of provenance can make attribution practically unavailable; multi-actor control ranks third because producer, deployer and clinician frequently control different risk points; warning and reliance, and causation under uncertainty follow because existing doctrines partly absorb them while leaving significant residual difficulty. The five gaps are therefore, in order of practical importance: evidence asymmetry (G1), documentation integrity (G5), multi-actor control (G3), warning and reliance (G6) and causation under uncertainty (G2). They are not evidence of legal emptiness. They are evidence of a mismatch between the evidential and organisational characteristics of healthcare AI deployments, on the one hand, and the architecture of the currently available compensation routes, on the other.Footnote 
<sup>8</sup>

The article is deliberately bounded. It is concerned with civil compensation routes and their interaction with sectoral regulation. It does not address criminal liability, professional discipline, GDPR claims as an autonomous pathway, insurance design or the full public-law enforcement architecture of the AI Act. The law-as-of date is 1 March 2026. The argument is not that the current framework is unworkable, nor that the withdrawn Directive would have solved everything. It is that the sharpest weaknesses lie at the junction between risk regulation and civil proof, and that this junction is especially visible in healthcare AI.

### 5. Implications for regulators, guidance bodies and public purchasers

 These three measures show that the most immediate response to the post-withdrawal liability landscape lies in upstream governance rather than in doctrinal development alone. That has implications for several actors. National competent authorities responsible for MDR and AI Act enforcement can treat traceability, retention and oversight design not merely as compliance matters, but as features that affect the reconstructability of harm events. Notified bodies can give closer attention to whether lifecycle documentation, instructions for use and post-market arrangements are sufficient to support patient-level incident reconstruction rather than only abstract conformity review. Guidance bodies such as HIQA-type quality agencies, the G-BA and AIFA-linked governance environments, and relevant professional bodies can frame procurement and deployment expectations in terms that connect safety governance with later accountability.Footnote 
<sup>56</sup>

 The accountability mechanisms created by the AI Act should be understood in the same setting. They include technical documentation, instructions for use, automatic logging, deployer monitoring and log retention, post-market monitoring, serious-incident reporting and, in limited Annex III settings, a right to an explanation of the AI system’s role in an individual decision. In the health sector, these mechanisms can make the relation between provider design choices, deployer use and clinical interpretation more traceable. Blatti and Tramacere’s analysis of transparency and liability in AI-based medical systems is useful here because it shows how transparency and human oversight can operate as accountability mechanisms before litigation begins, while remaining bounded by the scope of the AI Act and by the fact that regulatory accountability is not the same thing as civil liability.Footnote 
<sup>57</sup>
 For the purposes of the present article, this means that AI Act accountability mechanisms are not ignored. They are treated as part of the evidential and governance environment that can reduce opacity, support incident reconstruction and inform the standard of care through national mediating doctrines.

Large public purchasers have a particularly strong role. In concentrated markets, individual hospitals may lack leverage to insist on richer logging, provenance retention or audit access. Framework-level procurement, central guidance and collective contracting can change that bargaining position. The same is true of professional bodies that issue guidance on AI-enabled clinical tools. If their guidance remains at the level of general caution, it risks reproducing the warning-and-reliance gap. If, instead, it asks institutions to document control allocation, artefact retention and oversight realism, it can improve both governance and later legal clarity.

## V. What follows for risk regulation

### 1. An uneven but workable architecture

 The post-withdrawal landscape is uneven rather than empty. The revised Product Liability Directive improves the producer-side environment for software claims, particularly where classification, disclosure and presumptions matter. The AI Act, together with the MDR where applicable, improves the governance and evidential environment by requiring technical documentation, logs, instructions, post-market monitoring and oversight structures. Those are significant gains. Yet they do not create a general EU bridge between regulatory non-compliance and civil compensation, or displace the central role of national medical liability law, which remains the route through which most claimants will first proceed.Footnote 
<sup>52</sup>

 The unevenness is intensified by time. Many healthcare deployments already in use will not acquire richer AI Act artefacts merely because the Regulation exists. Some systems will fall outside the later high-risk obligations. Others will remain in service without the kind of significant change that would trigger application to pre-existing deployments. Still others will be formally in scope but unevenly compliant. The result is a patchwork in which some claimants benefit from richer logs, documentation and instructions, while others continue to depend on sparse records, proprietary environments and difficult counterfactuals. In that setting, risk regulation cannot be assessed only by asking whether it promotes *ex ante* safety or formal compliance. It must also be assessed by asking whether it leaves behind a litigation environment in which serious harms can be reconstructed and responsibility allocated with a reasonable degree of coherence.

### 3. G3: multi-actor control

The third gap is multi-actor control. Healthcare AI deployments distribute control across a chain of actors in ways that neither the product-liability route nor the provider-liability route maps neatly. The producer side may control design, training, performance claims and updates. The deployer may control procurement, threshold setting, workflow placement, local validation and incident response. The clinician may control final action or signature. In some cases, especially S3, a downstream clinician may act on information already shaped by the system without ever using the system directly. The legal question is not merely who caused the harm. It is which actor controlled the risk point that made the harm possible.

The structural character of G3 can be seen by comparing the scenarios. In S1, control is distributed, but the central contest is often still bilateral: producer design and updates against deployer workflow integration. In S2, threshold configuration introduces a more explicit allocation problem because the same model may behave differently depending on a parameter set locally rather than by the vendor. In S3, the chain expands again: producer-side note generation; provider-side procurement and governance; clinician review and signature; downstream clinician reliance. The ambient-scribe scenario therefore shows why control allocation is not only a product-liability issue or only a medical-liability issue. It is a chain problem.

 Ireland, Italy and Germany each provide partial but incomplete answers. Ireland’s law of concurrent wrongdoers and contribution can manage multi-defendant litigation after several parties have been joined, but it does not give a freestanding normative account of AI-mediated control allocation. Italy’s dual-track architecture is good at distinguishing institution and practitioner, but less obviously suited to integrating the producer side into the same conceptual frame. Germany’s doctrine is stronger in relation to organisational fault and to provider-side responsibility for documentation and process, but it too leaves unresolved the interface between producer control, deployer configuration and clinician use. The revised Product Liability Directive does not solve this problem, because it is still principally concerned with the producer side, even though it contains provisions on presentation as producer, related services and substantial modification.Footnote 
<sup>43</sup>
 The AI Act clarifies value-chain roles for regulatory purposes, including circumstances in which a deployer becomes a provider. But that is a public-law allocation of compliance responsibility, not a civil-law theory of multi-actor attribution.Footnote 
<sup>44</sup>

### 1. The claimant-facing problem after the withdrawal

 The withdrawal of the proposed AI Liability Directive did not create a legal vacuum.Footnote 
<sup>1</sup>
 It left in place a structured but uneven legal landscape in which a claimant who alleges harm caused by healthcare AI must route the case through three channels: strict product liability against the producer side; national fault-based liability against the provider side; and regulatory duties that matter to the evidential and normative environment, but do not themselves amount to a Union cause of action.Footnote 
<sup>2</sup>
 That architecture is workable in the limited sense that claims remain legally imaginable. It is less satisfactory in the practical sense that the route most visible to the claimant is often not the route that contains the decisive evidence. Patients usually know the hospital, clinic or the treating clinician. They rarely know who controlled the model version, the local alert threshold, the provenance trail, the audit log or the update history that later becomes determinative.

 Healthcare AI is a revealing test case because harm in this setting is usually mediated rather than immediate. In a radiology triage setting, the question is not simply whether an output was wrong, but whether the output altered worklist position, reporting time and therapeutic timing in a way that made a legally relevant difference. In a deterioration-score setting, the question is whether the model score, the local threshold and the escalation protocol altered admission, discharge or monitoring decisions. In an ambient scribe setting, the question is whether the system contaminated the medical record and whether that contamination later shaped clinical judgment. Liability therefore turns not only on AI error in the abstract, but on where the system sits in the clinical workflow, who controlled the relevant intervention point, and whether the system generated a retrievable evidential trace.Footnote 
<sup>3</sup>

### 4. G6: warning and reliance

 The fourth gap is the mismatch between formal warnings and real reliance patterns. In all three scenarios, the producer side can say that clinicians remain responsible, that outputs require review, and that the system is only assistive. In all three scenarios, the deployment may nonetheless be arranged so that the system predictably shapes clinician behaviour in ways stronger than those warnings imply. Hard worklist prioritisation makes non-prioritised cases less salient. Active alert architectures normalise reliance on the presence or absence of alerts. Auto-populated notes and medication fields reduce the intensity of human verification, especially where clinical work is fast-moving and documentation tasks are burdensome.Footnote 
<sup>45</sup>

 The structural issue is therefore not simply whether warnings existed, but whether they were consistent with the system’s real position in the workflow. This is why the gap is properly described as one of warning and reliance rather than as a simple failure of disclosure. If the system is built and deployed in a manner that makes superficial review or selective adherence foreseeable, the existence of a warning does not settle the safety or negligence question.Footnote 
<sup>46</sup>
 The revised Product Liability Directive reinforces this by expressly providing that warnings do not, by themselves, cure defectiveness. The AI Act reinforces it in a different way by requiring human oversight measures commensurate with risk, autonomy and context of use.Footnote 
<sup>47</sup>
 But neither instrument abolishes the behavioural gap. They help identify it; they do not make it disappear.

### 6. What the withdrawn Directive would and would not have solved

 The withdrawn Directive should therefore be understood with restraint. It would have addressed G1 and part of G2 by giving claimants a clearer route to producer-held evidence and by easing some causal proof under opacity. Those are precisely the points at which its absence is most clearly felt in healthcare AI cases. It would not have provided a complete theory of responsibility across the AI supply chain, and it would not have displaced the central role of national medical liability law. Multi-actor control would still have required national doctrines on negligence, contribution, organisational responsibility and clinical accountability. The Directive’s value lay in targeted procedural assistance, not in replacing that wider legal landscape.Footnote 
<sup>58</sup>

 That bounded claim matters for risk regulation. It prevents the current debate from collapsing into a false choice between “more AI-specific liability law” and “no legal problem.” The post-withdrawal framework already contains meaningful resources, and the revised Product Liability Directive and the AI Act improve the position, though unevenly. But their combination still leaves the claimant exposed where the decisive artefact sits outside ordinary reach, where provenance was not preserved, where control is distributed across several actors, and where the main negligence route still bears the weight of causal uncertainty. The task for risk regulation is therefore not only to reduce harm *ex ante*. It is also to leave behind a legal and evidential environment in which harms that do occur can be reconstructed with tolerable clarity.

On 11 February 2025, the European Commission formally withdrew its proposal for an AI Liability Directive (COM/2022/496), first presented in September 2022 as the civil-liability counterpart to the EU AI Act. The proposal was never adopted, so none of its provisions ever took effect. The withdrawal, however, does not leave a liability vacuum: liability for harm caused by artificial intelligence systems is now governed, at EU level, by the revised Product Liability Directive – Directive (EU) 2024/2853, adopted on 23 October 2024. This piece examines why the AI Liability Directive was withdrawn, what the new liability regime actually provides, and what it means in practice for businesses placing AI products or services on the EU market.

### Why the AI Liability Directive was withdrawn?

The European Commission justified the withdrawal by the absence of any realistic prospect of agreement on a final text within a reasonable timeframe – the decision was taken as part of the Commission’s 2025 Work Programme. The proposal had been built around a fault-based liability model, requiring an injured party to prove a breach on the part of the AI provider or manufacturer. The Commission concluded that the revised Product Liability Directive, which explicitly brings software – including AI systems – within the definition of a product, adequately covers the same ground, rendering a separate directive unnecessary.

 The older CJEU case law retains interpretive force across the legacy regime. Veedfald confirms that a medical product can be put into circulation even in a hospital-linked context. Ford Italia reinforces the breadth of the concept of producer by presentation. Boston Scientific remains central to heightened safety expectations for medical products. Commission v United Kingdom and Commission v France continue to frame the development-risk defence by reference to the objective state of scientific and technical knowledge. Sanofi Pasteur accepts proof through serious, specific and consistent indicia rather than scientific certainty, while rejecting automatic or irrebuttable presumptions. Novo Nordisk confirms that national information-access tools may coexist with the product liability regime. Dutrueux makes clear that the harmonised product route coexists with national fault-based liability where the latter rests on a different basis.Footnote 
<sup>26</sup>
 Product liability therefore remains a viable but incomplete route for healthcare AI claims. It is strongest where the producer side is identifiable, the system is comfortably classifiable as a product, and the decisive artefacts exist and can be reached.

 Lens B improves the claimant’s position in product claims through Article 10 presumptions, including the rule for excessive difficulties in establishing defectiveness or causation in technically complex cases.Footnote 
<sup>51</sup>
 That is a substantial change, especially for producer-side claims involving opaque software. But it does not extend to the negligence or treatment-contract route against the hospital, which often remains the first and most practical claimant route. The AI Act also helps only in part. Better logging can illuminate the first node in the chain, such as whether an alert fired or whether a record was generated. It does not by itself answer the later counterfactuals, whether a clinician would have acted differently, whether a different action would have occurred in time, and whether outcome would thereby have changed. G2 therefore persists because the main fault-based route continues to depend on proof structures that the new product-liability tools cannot fully reach.

 The sensitivity of G5 to regulation is more differentiated than that of G1. The AI Act can reduce documentation-integrity problems substantially, but only where the system falls within scope, the relevant provisions have begun to apply, and the deployment is compliant. Article 12 requires logging, and Article 26 requires deployers to keep automatically generated logs for a minimum period.Footnote 
<sup>41</sup>
 For medical device AI, the MDR also brings traceability and post-market documentation into the picture. Recent MDCG guidance reinforces the importance of traceability, transparency and human oversight in medical device AI and links them to accountability across the lifecycle.Footnote 
<sup>42</sup>
 Yet it would be too broad to say that documentation-integrity problems disappear under the later regime. The ambient-scribe setting may fall outside MDR classification; the relevant AI Act provisions may not yet apply; and compliant high-level logging does not necessarily guarantee retention of the exact pre-edit draft or the patient-level provenance detail that litigation later demands. G5 is therefore best described as materially reducible, not removable, by later regulation.

### 2. National fault-based routes in Ireland, Italy and Germany

 The second surviving channel is national fault-based liability. In practice, it is often the first channel activated because the institution is visible, record-holding and usually solvent or indemnified. In Ireland, the relevant standard in clinical negligence remains the Dunne standard, as restated in later case law including Morrissey. Discovery under Order 31 remains comparatively broad, including the possibility of third-party discovery, although the practical and strategic value of that route in technically complex cases should not be overstated.Footnote 
<sup>27</sup>
 Irish causation remains demanding. *Philp v Ryan* and *Quinn v Mid-Western Health Board* are both relevant, but it is safer to describe them as evidence of an unsettled landscape regarding expanded causation tools than as settling any specific material-contribution doctrine for AI-mediated clinical harm.Footnote 
<sup>28</sup>

 Italy’s position is shaped by Law 24/2017. The healthcare facility is liable on a contractual footing, while the practitioner is generally liable extra-contractually under Article 2043 of the Civil Code. Product liability claims continue to proceed under the Consumer Code. The Corte di Cassazione has recently reaffirmed, in Cass. civ., Sez. III, 28 March 2025, n 8224, that the product-liability regime does not exclude or limit other liability routes, but that distinct regimes cannot simply be blended into one another. In the same decision, the Court again described product liability as a form of *responsabilità presunta*, literally “presumed liability,” rather than true objective liability.Footnote 
<sup>29</sup>
 Causation remains governed by the more-probable-than-not standard, and the court-appointed expert mechanism (*consulenza tecnica d’ufficio*, CTU) continues to play a large role in structuring medical and technical proof.Footnote 
<sup>30</sup>

## VI. Conclusion

Healthcare AI claims do not succeed or fail because of abstract positions about artificial intelligence. They turn on more concrete questions: whether the system is clearly classifiable as a product; whether the decisive artefact exists; who controlled the risk point that mattered; whether workflow design undermined formal warnings; and whether the claimant can prove a multi-step counterfactual against parties holding different fragments of the evidence. Across Ireland, Italy and Germany, those questions produce different doctrinal routes but recognisably similar structural frictions.

The revised Product Liability Directive improves the producer-side landscape for software products and for technically difficult proof. The AI Act, together with the MDR where applicable, improves the governance and evidential setting, sometimes substantially. Yet the claimant-facing weakness exposed by the withdrawal of the AI Liability Directive remains visible where evidence is vendor-held, where provenance was never retained, where control was distributed across several actors, and where negligence-side causation still carries much of the burden. The present architecture is therefore workable, but imperfect. Its sharpest weaknesses lie at the junction between risk regulation and civil proof.

 The contribution of this article is to show, through healthcare AI, that this junction is where the law now does much of its most difficult work. The post-withdrawal position is neither a void nor a complete settlement. It is an uneven architecture in which *ex ante* regulation and *ex post* compensation no longer move in step. If there is a practical lesson to draw, it is that liability readiness now depends as much on procurement design, retention architecture and workflow realism as on doctrinal elegance.

### 1. Product liability under Lens A and Lens B

 The first surviving channel is strict product liability against the producer side. Under Lens A, the claimant proceeds under Directive 85/374/EEC as transposed into national law. Under Lens B, the claimant proceeds under Directive (EU) 2024/2853. In healthcare AI, the difference between the two is not merely technical. It affects whether software supplied through cloud or software-as-a-service models is comfortably classified as a product; how much procedural assistance is available where proof depends on producer-held evidence; and how the law responds to post-deployment software change, updates and continued producer control.Footnote 
<sup>18</sup>

 Under Lens B, software is expressly included as a product, whether supplied on a tangible medium or through network access, cloud or software-as-a-service models.Footnote 
<sup>19</sup>
 This matters most for the ambient clinical scribe. If the scribe is not a medical device, its treatment under Lens A remains more contestable because older national implementations were drafted against a world of tangible goods and do not uniformly resolve the status of cloud-delivered software. Under Lens B that uncertainty is greatly reduced. The revised Directive also addresses related services and substantial modification, which is relevant where functionality is altered through software updates or ongoing learning processes beyond the user’s control.Footnote 
<sup>20</sup>

 Across both lenses, the organising concept remains defectiveness, assessed by reference to the safety that a person is entitled to expect. CJEU case law has long recognised that, for medical products, safety expectations are especially demanding because the potential damage is abnormal and serious.Footnote 
<sup>21</sup>
 The revised Directive deepens the contextual analysis by making explicit that defectiveness may depend on continuing learning, interconnection with other products, cybersecurity and the circumstances of the intended user group.Footnote 
<sup>22</sup>
 It also makes clear that warnings do not, by themselves, cure defectiveness, a proposition with direct relevance to systems that are formally described as assistive but are designed in ways that predictably induce reliance.Footnote 
<sup>23</sup>

### 5. G2: causation under uncertainty

The fifth gap is causation under uncertainty. Healthcare AI harms rarely present a short path from technical event to injury. In S1, a low-priority triage output may delay review; the delay may postpone diagnosis; the postponement may or may not have altered treatment or outcome. In S2, an alert that did not fire, or did not cross a threshold, may affect escalation, monitoring or discharge; each step is contestable in clinical and evidential terms. In S3, a contaminated note may shape later clinical understanding, but only through a chain involving authorship, review, reliance and the timing of later investigation. Each of these cases requires the claimant to stabilise a counterfactual across several actors and several decision points.

 The three jurisdictions differ sharply here. Ireland remains the least claimant-friendly of the three because the but-for test continues to dominate clinical negligence, and the law is still unsettled as to how far expanded causation tools can travel in medical settings. Philp and Quinn do not resolve the matter in a way that maps neatly onto AI-mediated chains, and Morrissey does not remove that underlying difficulty.Footnote 
<sup>50</sup>
 Italy’s more-probable-than-not standard and the burden structure of Law 24/2017 soften the edges of uncertainty, especially as against the healthcare facility, but they do not by themselves solve multi-link chains involving producer-side evidence gaps. Germany offers the strongest statutory assistance through section 630h, yet even there the assistance is usually strongest on the provider side and weaker when the contested issue concerns producer-side design, provenance or calibration.
